standard.title: Analysing Information and Perspectives
standard.description: analyse information, data and ideas about political, legal or civic issues to identify and explain differences in perspectives and potential challenges
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can evaluate information to identify patterns, trends, and relationships (AC9HS6S03) and evaluate sources and perspectives (AC9HS6S04). The Y7 shift is to explicitly civic analytical work — identifying how perspectives on political and legal issues differ and why, and what challenges arise from this.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse information, data and ideas about civic issues to identify and explain differences in perspectives and potential challenges.

nodes.label: Identifying perspectives in civic sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the perspective expressed in a civic source — who produced it, what position it represents, and how this shapes the information it contains.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the source of a piece of civic information (e.g. government website, newspaper editorial, advocacy group report), describe whose perspective it represents, and explain how that perspective might shape the information.
nodes.typical_width: Examine online publications or media reports and identify the perspective each represents; explain how a government source, a civil society source, and a media source on the same issue might present the information differently; identify whose perspective might be absent from each source.
wider: Compare multiple sources on the same civic issue (e.g. court system reform) from different institutional perspectives — government, legal profession, advocacy group, media — to map the range of viewpoints
Investigate how the framing of a civic issue (e.g. which facts are emphasised, what language is used) reflects the perspective of the source
Explore how First Nations Australians' perspectives on civic issues (e.g. land rights, constitutional recognition) may differ from mainstream government or media coverage of those issues
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying perspective is the prerequisite for explaining differences between perspectives — students who cannot see a source as a positioned view rather than neutral information cannot meaningfully compare perspectives or identify challenges.

response_modes.reason: The move from 'what does this source say' to 'whose perspective does this source represent and how does that shape it' is a genuine conceptual step — invest in this distinction explicitly before moving to comparison.

success_criteria: Identify the perspective represented by a civic source and explain how that perspective might influence the information it contains
Identify at least one perspective that might be absent from a given source

nodes.label: Comparing and explaining perspective differences
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare the perspectives of different sources on the same civic issue and explain why their views differ.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two sources with different perspectives on the same civic issue and explain at least one reason why their views differ.
nodes.typical_width: Compare perspectives from multiple sources on a civic issue (e.g. a Lowy Institute poll vs a government statement vs media coverage); explain what causes perspective differences (different values, interests, access to information, institutional roles); draw preliminary conclusions about the issue based on this comparison.
wider: Evaluate which perspective is better supported by evidence for a given civic claim, distinguishing between value-based disagreements and factual disagreements
Investigate a civic issue where perspectives have changed over time (e.g. public views on same-sex marriage, Indigenous rights) to understand how perspectives evolve
Analyse data from surveys or polls (e.g. Lowy Institute, ABS) and compare the findings with qualitative perspectives from media or advocacy sources

response_modes.reason: Using a range of civic issues for perspective comparison (not just one case study) builds transferability — students need to practise the comparison skill across different types of civic questions (legal, governmental, social cohesion).

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The distinction between value-based and factual disagreements in civic debates is a genuinely sophisticated analytical move — students who can identify this distinction understand the structure of civic controversy rather than just cataloguing different views.
success_criteria: Compare the perspectives of two sources on the same civic issue and identify at least one point of agreement and one of disagreement
Explain at least one reason why the perspectives differ

nodes.label: Identifying potential challenges
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify potential challenges arising from perspective differences in civic issues — including challenges for policy, governance, social cohesion, or legal application.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one potential challenge arising from competing perspectives on a civic issue (e.g. how to balance freedom of speech with the right to be protected from harmful speech).
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a civic issue to identify potential challenges arising from competing perspectives; explain what makes the challenge difficult to resolve (e.g. competing values, different stakeholder interests, gaps in evidence); connect the challenge to the broader system (legal, democratic, social) it arises within.
wider: Evaluate the court system's effectiveness by comparing perspectives of those who have used it, legal professionals, and reform advocates — drawing conclusions about systemic challenges

Investigate a contemporary civic challenge (e.g. balancing security and civil liberties, managing political misinformation) where perspectives genuinely conflict and identify what would need to change for progress
Explore how challenges to civic participation — barriers faced by different groups — create systemic issues for democratic representation

response_modes.reason: Identifying challenges requires integrating perspective analysis with knowledge of civic systems — students apply what they know about the legal or democratic system to diagnose why a particular challenge is hard to resolve.

success_criteria: Identify at least one potential challenge arising from competing perspectives on a civic issue
Explain what makes the challenge difficult to resolve with reference to the perspectives involved
